body.text: Okinawa’s new governor had barely begun his effort to improve relations with Tokyo when an alleged killing involving a U.S. Marine confronted him with the prefecture’s most persistent political dilemma: how to support national defense while protecting residents who bear a disproportionate share of its costs.

Okinawa Prefectural Police arrested Lance Corporal Devin Jacob Ballard, 20, stationed at Marine Corps Air Station Futenma, early on October 4. He is suspected of killing Yagi Anna, a 39-year-old Naha resident, at a hotel and stealing her belongings. Ballard denies the allegations. The Marine Corps has pledged cooperation with Japanese investigators.

The case immediately drew protests from both national and prefectural authorities. Foreign Minister Motegi Toshimitsu summoned U.S. Ambassador George Glass, while Defense Minister Koizumi Shinjiro summoned U.S. Forces Japan commander Lieutenant General Stephen Jost.

On October 5, before delivering her policy speech to the Diet, Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae condemned the incident and demanded full investigative cooperation, tighter discipline, and effective measures to prevent further crimes.
For Governor Koja Genta, who took office on September 30, the timing was especially difficult.

His September 13 election ended 12 years of prefectural leadership opposed to relocating Futenma to Henoko in northern Okinawa. Koja has sought a more cooperative relationship with Tokyo. Effective October 1, he replaced the prefectural division handling opposition to the Henoko project with an office focused on accelerating the return of U.S. military land.
But his cooperation was never unconditional. Koja has acknowledged the need for defense capabilities while demanding advance explanations and local understanding.

In a protest letter read aloud to Lieutenant General Benjamin Watson, commander of III Marine Expeditionary Force, and U.S. Consul General Andrew Ou on October 5, Koja said that the recurrence of such a serious crime “leads us to conclude that U.S. military efforts regarding discipline and human rights education are completely ineffective.” He demanded stronger preventive measures and a review of the Japan-U.S. Status of Forces Agreement, or SOFA.
Watson expressed condolences and pledged continued cooperation with the investigation, saying the U.S. military was committed to being “good neighbors” and earning the trust of the Okinawan people.
That exchange reflects a longstanding problem.

Okinawa hosts approximately 70 percent of Japan’s nationwide area of facilities reserved exclusively for U.S. military use. Residents thus experience the alliance through noise, accidents, environmental concerns, and criminal cases, alongside its promised protection against external threats.

In 2025, police cleared 101 cases involving Penal Code offenses by U.S. military personnel, civilian employees, and their families, up from 73 in 2024. These figures count cases, not convictions or individual offenders, and do not establish a comparative crime rate. Nevertheless, there is good reason for scrutinizing measures introduced after earlier incidents, including restrictions on nighttime drinking and joint patrols.

Japan generally has primary jurisdiction over off-duty offenses against Japanese nationals. When American authorities already hold a suspect, however, the SOFA provides for U.S. custody until indictment. Following the 1995 rape of a schoolgirl by three U.S. servicemen, Washington agreed to give “sympathetic consideration” to Japanese requests for pre-indictment transfers in murder and rape cases.

Ballard was arrested by Japanese police and remains in Japanese custody. This is therefore not a case of Washington withholding a suspect. The broader question is whether existing arrangements under the SOFA provide sufficient accountability, information sharing, and preventive oversight.

The controversy comes as Japan’s defense buildup in its southwestern islands enters a more operational phase. Tokyo is connecting missile deployments, surveillance, transport, and logistics across Kyushu and the southwestern islands, while U.S. forces develop more dispersed operations.

Plans to store the U.S. Army’s Typhon and HIMARS systems at Kadena and deploy Marine NMESIS anti-ship missiles and MADIS air defense systems to Ishigaki during October’s Keen Sword exercise make cooperation with local authorities particularly consequential. Koja has so far withheld judgment on the storage plan, saying Tokyo has not adequately explained the reasons or its duration.

Koja’s election gave Tokyo reason to expect smoother negotiations. It did not give the Japanese government or the U.S. military a blank check. Anger over this case could make individual decisions on facilities, exercises, and base restructuring politically harder, even without reversing Japan’s overall defense policy.

For Koja, the test is whether cooperation with Tokyo and Washington can produce tangible protection for Okinawans. For the alliance, the stakes are broader: deterrence in Japan’s southwest depends not only on missiles, bases, and military units, but also on the trust of the communities expected to host them.
